Methods and results In this randomized, single-blinded clinical trial, 201 patients (non-fasting = 100, fasting = 101) with a mean age of 72.0 + 11.6 years (66.7% male) were assigned to a non-fasting strategy (solids/ fl uids allowed up to 1 h) or a fasting strategy (at least 6 h no solids and 2 h no fl uids) before the procedure and analysed on an intention-to-treat basis. The co-primary outcomes were patients ' well-being scores (based on numeric rating scale, 0 -10) and incidence of intra-procedural food-related adverse events, including vomiting, perioperative pulmonary aspiration, and emergency intubation. Renal, haematological, and metabolic blood parameters and 30-day follow-up data were gathered. The summed pre-procedural patients ' well-being score was signi fi cantly lower in the non-fasting group [non-fasting: 13.1 + 9.6 vs. fasting: 16.5 + 11.4, 95% con fi dence interval (CI) of mean difference (MD) -6.35 to -0.46, P = 0.029], which was mainly driven by signi fi cantly lower scores for hunger and tiredness in the non-fasting group (non-fasting vs. fasting; hunger: 0.9 + 1.9 vs. 3.1 + 3.2, 95% CI of MD -2.86 to -1.42, P , 0.001; tiredness: 1.6 + 2.3 vs. 2.6 + 2.7, 95% CI of MD -1.68 to -0.29, P = 0.023). No intra-procedural food-related adverse events were observed. Relevant blood parameters and 30-day follow-up did not show signi fi cant differences.

texts.orig: Pre-procedural fasting has often been practiced for about 4 -6 h before interventional cardiac procedures, such as percutaneous coronary interventions and implantation of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs). However, extended fasting may occur when these procedures are delayed or cancelled. 1 Requiring patients to have a strict 6-h fasting window for solid food also hinders scheduling patients for earlier appointments if schedule changes.

texts.orig: Prolonged fasting may exacerbate the organic response to trauma by increasing insulin resistance, gluconeogenesis, and acute-phase response; it leaves patients often dissatis fi ed and adds to the discomfort and anxiety of waiting for a procedure. 2 Moreover, patients under fasting are potentially at risk of dehydration, contrast-induced nephropathy, hypoglycaemia, and poorly controlled hypertension, particularly in the older age group. 3

texts.orig: The primary concept of pre-operative fasting was instituted between 1855 and 1945 when anaesthetic techniques were rudimentary, and chloroform was used. Nausea, vomiting, and aspiration were feared. 4,5 However, current guidelines reveal the absence of a strong association between fasting, gastric volume, or risk of nausea, vomiting, and aspiration. 6 Pre-procedural fasting practice varies substantially between interventional cardiologists, and the available evidence to guide the correct practice is also limited. 7

These procedures are mainly performed under local anaesthesia without or with only slight anxiolytic sedation and analgesia.

texts.orig: The CIED procedure was performed in both groups according to current standards, and every patient received antibiotic prophylaxis. 9,10 Local anaesthesia with 20 -40 mL Mepivacaine 1% was administered to the operation site. Depending on the patient ' s needs, additional administration of intravenous analgesics (fentanyl) and sedatives (midazolam, rarely Propofol) was possible to achieve minimal to moderate sedation with at least adequate spontaneous ventilation, maintained cardiovascular function, and purposeful response to verbal or tactile stimulation, 11 meaning that protective re fl exes were maintained. After infraclavicular incision and mostly subcutaneous pocket preparation (subpectoral preparation in cachexia or existing subpectoral device-pocket), cephalic vein or subclavian vein was used for lead access. Subcutaneous and intracutaneous absorbable sutures were used for wound closure. No de fi brillation tests in implantable cardioverter de fi brillator recipients were made. The duration of the CIED procedure was de fi ned as the time between the fi rst incision and the last suture.

Medications given during the CIED procedure by the nursing staff following the surgeon ' s guidelines were collected and categorized into sedatives, analgetics, and antiemetics. Any intra-procedural adverse events, including emergency intubation, perioperative pulmonary aspiration, and vomiting, were recorded.

The NRS levels were used to classify three pain categories low/moderate/severe (NRS 0 -3, 4 -5, 6 -10), respectively. These categories were also used to classify patients ' well-being scores. texts.orig: This study showed that a non-fasting strategy is advantageous compared with a fasting strategy regarding patient ' s well-being and comparable in terms of safety for patients undergoing elective CIED procedures. To our knowledge, this is the fi rst randomized clinical study to assess the bene fi ts of a non-fasting strategy for an interventional cardiac procedure. The summed pre-procedural well-being score was signi fi cantly lower for the non-fasting group, which re fl ects more well-being in this group which was mainly driven by signi fi cantly lower scores for hunger and tiredness in the non-fasting group. Non-fasting before CIED procedures did not in fl uence renal, metabolic, and haematological blood parameters and duration of hospital stay. No intra-procedural foodintake-related incidents concerning vomiting, aspiration, or emergency intubation were observed in both groups. The study also showed that, in daily practice, fasting times for patients were longer than intended.

texts.orig: The fi rst attempt to assess the clinical application of non-fasting before cardiac interventions was conducted by Hamid et al . 3 in 2014. In this retrospective analysis of 2000 percutaneous coronary interventions, reports of bronchial aspiration, aspiration pneumonia, or intra-procedural intubation over a 3-year period were lacking. 3 Studies about non-cardiac procedures, such as abdominal surgery, 8 -15 thyroidectomy, 16 or elective ophthalmologic surgery, 17 showed that shortened pre-operative fasting or supplying patients with a carbohydrate-loaded drink 2 h before the procedures is safe and decreased parameters, such as post-operative nausea and vomiting, hospital stay, insulin resistance, and increased well-being. Although most of these procedures required at least deep sedation and in fl icted more physical trauma on the body than CIED procedures, the bene fi cial effects of a non-fasting strategy can be assumed to be comparable with other cardiac interventional procedures, such as those in our trial. Even if many patients are overweight, fasting before surgery is not an adequate time to start with weight loss, as it increases insulin resistance, disrupts intra-cellular calcium homeostasis, 18 and provokes mental and physical stress, which might be detrimental to the recovery process. The assessed levels for hunger and tiredness differed signi fi cantly, with lower scores for the non-fasting group. Other well-being factors for patients, such as pain, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, and thirst before the procedure, were not signi fi cantly different. This is not surprising, as even patients scheduled for fasting were allowed to drink for up to 2 h until the procedure. Hunger being higher in fasting patients is also expected. However, although this difference is statistically signi fi cant, the actual values for both groups are not very high. It is possible that during questioning, which occurred before the start of the CIED procedure, patients were too nervous or excited, which decreased their feelings of hunger. There are a few studies investigating well-being parameters in the fi eld of non-cardiac interventions, which showed, depending on the investigated items, more hunger, thirst, mouth dryness, headache, tiredness, weakness, and inability to concentrate in overnight fasted patients compared with patients prepared with carbohydrate drinks 2 h before surgery. 16,17 In contrast to these studies, non-fasting patients in our study were allowed to eat and drink up to an hour before surgery and were not provided with mandatory carbohydrate drinks.

texts.orig: Incidents of vomiting/aspiration during the procedures in this trial were lacking. Post-procedural respiratory infections might be a sequel of (silent) aspirations and were therefore collected in this study, but were unremarkable. Overall, the rate of intra-operative aspiration has been reported to be between 1:7000 19 and 3:10 000, 20 which is mainly in procedures with at least deep sedation. Additionally, the actual mortality of aspiration due to the therapeutic advantages of antibiotics has considerably decreased during the last decades. Therefore, it is questionable whether the minor bene fi t of less gastric content in the rare case of aspiration is relevant enough to keep a patient fasting for a long time when long periods of fasting also incur other risks and increase feelings of discomfort, such as hunger and tiredness. This is especially true for procedures where patients are in control of their re fl exes and are not intubated, such as the patients collected for this study. A study by Manchikanti et al . 13 showed that, for 18 472 nonfasting interventional procedures in 3179 patients with mostly conscious or intravenous sedation, only very few patients (189 of 11 856 encounters, 1.6%) complained of nausea after the procedure. Vomiting occurred in only three patients. No aspiration effects were described within all procedures. 13

texts.orig: Notably, real fasting times for both groups were longer than the minimum demands. Fasting times were , 2 h for 32 and , 3 h for 42 patients in the non-fasting group. Meal serving times in hospitals are mainly standardized, regardless of the procedure starting time. Last meals are mainly served in the evening. Patients who are scheduled for the fi rst procedure in the morning, before/during breakfast is served, have therefore fasted much longer. Studies on fasting time in real practice are rare. 1,13 Our data agree with a study by Chon et al ., 14 demonstrating that delays, schedule changes, and errors often occur and induce increased fasting time, with 12.8 + 2.2 h of average fasting before a procedure, similar to our fasting group, and an additional 2.5 + 1.7 h, if delayed. This means that even with a non-fasting policy, some patients will appear during the CIED procedure with longer fasting hours.
